item.title: Millions in Fangaʻuta bridge penalties mount as PM reveals more land issues delaying construction
item.description: Tonga continues to face mounting financial costs from delays to the US$97 million Fangaʻuta Lagoon bridge project, as more unresolved land disputes prevent construction from moving forward about a year after the contract was signed. item.content:encoded:
Tonga continues to face mounting financial costs from delays to the US$97 million Fangaʻuta Lagoon bridge project, as more unresolved land disputes prevent construction from moving forward about a year after the contract was signed.

The continuing disputes have left the government negotiating with landowners over compensation and other matters that Fakafanua said should have been resolved before the contract was signed and before the New Zealand contractor was allowed to mobilise to Tonga.

Fakafanua said land negotiations were among the most difficult aspects of the process and should have been settled beforehand. The bridge construction contract was signed at a ceremony presided over by the King.

Signed in September 2025 by the former ʻAisake Eke government and McConnell Dowell Constructors Ltd, the project includes a 720-metre bridge across Fangaʻuta Lagoon and 2.1 kilometres of approach roads linking Nukuʻalofa with southern Tongatapu. Completion is scheduled for the end of 2028.

As Kaniva News recently reported, former Infrastructure Minister Sēmisi Sika said in an interview with us that the project’s main construction phase remained on hold because of unresolved land issues at ʻUmusī, where the northern end of the bridge is expected to begin.

He said the contractor was carrying out preliminary work where possible, but construction across the lagoon could not begin until the land issues were settled.

The prolonged delay has resulted in substantial financial penalties for the government. Sika said about $7 million in penalty fees were paid during the six months from September 2025 to February 2026.

With the land issues unresolved and construction yet to begin, Sika said the government was likely to incur another $7 million in penalties over the following six months through August, potentially bringing the total to $14 million.

Lord Fakafanua later confirmed at a press conference that the government had received the claims from McConnell Dowell, but said there was a possibility of reducing the amount through a value engineering process that could lower the costs of some materials.

However, the Prime Minister told TBC’s Viola Ulakai during a livestreamed interview this week that he had recently discovered there were also land issues at Lord Veikune’s Longoteme lands near Folaha, where the southern section of the bridge is planned, with compensation negotiations yet to be settled.

This comes amid negotiations over affected land ‘Umusī also remain unresolved.

The latest comments come after Kaniva News sought clarification from Lord Fakafanua regarding conflicting public statements on the project’s progress, compensation claims, project costs, and the status of the land disputes.

We also sought confirmation of reports that a landowner at ʻUmusī was seeking $10 million in compensation from the government and that a Chinese business owner leasing part of the affected land was seeking a further $12 million.

Among the questions was whether relocating the bridge’s starting point away from the disputed area would remove the reported $22 million compensation claim and whether any agreement had been reached with the affected parties.

Kaniva News also requested clarification over the cost of the ongoing delays.

We also asked Lord Fakafanua whether he would seek any compensation or lease arrangement for the use of land within his estate at ʻUmusī, where part of the bridge is expected to pass.

As of publication, the Prime Minister’s Office had not responded to those questions.

Kaniva News remains willing to publish any response from the Prime Minister or the government as soon as it is received.

item.title: Princess Angelika, PM Fakafanua honour Taumalolo’s 300-game milestone in Townsville
item.description: Townsville, Australia – Tonga’s pride in one of its greatest sporting figures was evident today as Her Royal Highness Princess Angelika Lātūfuipeka Tukuʻaho and Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua travelled to Townsville to honour rugby league star Jason Taumalolo on the occasion of his 300th National Rugby League (NRL) match. item.content:encoded:
Townsville, Australia – Tonga’s pride in one of its greatest sporting figures was evident today as Her Royal Highness Princess Angelika Lātūfuipeka Tukuʻaho and Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua travelled to Townsville to honour rugby league star Jason Taumalolo on the occasion of his 300th National Rugby League (NRL) match.

Their presence highlighted the national significance of the milestone, recognising Taumalolo not only as an elite athlete but also as a proud ambassador of Tonga on the world stage. The visit reflected the Kingdom’s deep appreciation for the achievements of its people abroad, particularly in rugby league where Tongans have made a powerful impact.

Taumalolo reached the historic milestone while playing for the North Queensland Cowboys against the Penrith Panthers at Queensland Country Bank Stadium. At 33 years of age, he became the first player in the club’s history to reach 300 NRL games, and only the 56th player in the competition’s long history to achieve the feat.

The achievement marks the culmination of a remarkable 16-year career that began when Taumalolo moved to Townsville as a 13-year-old with immense promise. He made his NRL debut in 2010 at just 17 years and two months, quickly emerging as one of the most formidable young talents in the game.

Over the years, Taumalolo has developed into one of rugby league’s most dominant forwards. Known for his explosive power, relentless work rate, and ability to break through defensive lines, he has redefined the modern lock forward role and earned widespread respect across the sport.

A key element of his legacy is his loyalty to the North Queensland Cowboys, having spent his entire NRL career with the club. He played a crucial role in their 2015 premiership victory and has remained one of the team’s most influential figures ever since.

Beyond club football, Taumalolo’s decision to represent Tonga internationally marked a turning point for Pacific rugby league. His leadership and commitment helped elevate Tonga into a competitive force on the global stage, inspiring pride among Tongans worldwide.

For Tonga, Taumalolo’s 300th match is more than a sporting milestone. It represents the success of a proud son of the nation whose achievements continue to uplift and unite the Tongan community at home and across the diaspora.

The celebrations in Townsville were marked by strong support from Tongan fans, many proudly displaying their national colours, creating a vibrant atmosphere that reflected the deep cultural connection to the occasion.

As Jason Taumalolo reaches this historic milestone, his legacy is firmly established as one of the greatest forwards in rugby league history. His journey stands as a testament to dedication, resilience, and the enduring strength of Tongan identity on the global stage.

item.title: Chinese Embassy says no evidence of human trafficking in response to viral livestream allegations
item.description: The Chinese Embassy in Tonga says there is currently no evidence to support claims of human trafficking following a viral Facebook livestream alleging that Tongan women had been lured to China for forced marriage. In a statement issued after the livestream attracted widespread attention on social media, the embassy said it was working with the Embassy of Tonga in China to investigate the matter.
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese Embassy in Tonga says there is currently no evidence to support claims of human trafficking following a viral Facebook livestream alleging that Tongan women had been lured to China for forced marriage.

In a statement issued after the livestream attracted widespread attention on social media, the embassy said it was working with the Embassy of Tonga in China to investigate the matter.

“Based on information available so far, the issue appears to be transnational marriage disputes,” the statement said.

The embassy said Chinese police were providing assistance to the three Tongan women referred to in the allegations and that, based on the information currently available, there was no evidence verifying that human trafficking was involved.

It added that if any unlawful conduct or non-compliance were identified on the Chinese side, the women’s legitimate rights and interests would be protected under Chinese law.

The embassy’s response follows a Facebook livestream on Wednesday by Tongan woman Aloi Katoa, who alleged that three Tongan women had travelled to China for marriage and later encountered serious difficulties.

The livestream quickly gained widespread attention, attracting more than 170,000 views and over 3,000 shares within hours of being posted.

The allegations prompted concern among members of the Tongan community, with many calling for authorities to investigate the claims.

The Chinese Embassy encouraged the women involved or their family members to contact officials directly to assist with ongoing enquiries.

Anyone with relevant information is encouraged to contact the Chinese Embassy in Tonga on +676 24-554, by email at chinaemb_to@mfa.gov.cn , or the Embassy of Tonga in China.

Kaniva News will continue to follow developments as more information becomes available.
